## Introduction

This tutorial covers key concepts from [Chapter 22: Arrow](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/arrow.html), [Chapter 19: Joins](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/joins.html), and [Chapter 17: Dates and times](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/datetimes.html) from [*R for Data Science (2e)*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund.

A prediction market lets people bet on whether a future event will happen. Each trade moves the price toward the bettor's belief, so the current price reads as the crowd's estimate of the probability. You will work with four parquet files describing 800 resolved markets and 43,694 daily probability snapshots, reading them with **[arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/)**, and finish with two charts: one asking whether forecasts sharpen as the deadline nears, and one asking whether a market that says 70% is right about 70% of the time.

Use AI however you like.

###

The data comes from **Manifold Markets**, a play-money platform launched in 2022. Traders use Mana, a fictional currency, which matters for how you read the results: nobody is risking rent on these forecasts, so the incentive to be right is weaker than on a real-money exchange like Kalshi or Polymarket.

Parquet stores a table column-by-column rather than row-by-row, so a query that touches one column reads only that column's bytes, and repeated values inside a column compress well. It shows in this data: 43,694 daily snapshots occupy 186 KB.

## Does the crowd get it right?

In this section you will join four parquet files representing 800 resolved markets and 43,694 daily probability snapshots to answer one question: as the resolution date approaches and more information becomes available, does the crowd get smarter?

Create the main forecasting table in that chunk. Read the market-level file into memory, attach the market outcome to each daily probability snapshot, and add an `outcome_numeric` field coded as 1 for YES and 0 for NO so errors can be calculated later. ```{r}

```{r}
  "Create the main forecasting table in that chunk. Read the market-level file into memory, attach the market outcome to each daily probability snapshot, and add an outcome_numeric field coded as 1 for YES and 0 for NO so errors can be calculated later. Save the result as joined and print the row count as a join check. Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: crowd-2-answer
#| echo: true
markets <- read_parquet("data/markets.parquet")

joined <- open_dataset("data/history.parquet") |>
  collect() |>
  left_join(markets, by = "market_id") |>
  mutate(outcome_numeric = if_else(outcome == "YES", 1, 0))

joined |> nrow()
```

###

The row count does not change: this is a one-to-many join, with one market row matched to many daily history rows, so each of the 43,694 history rows simply gains its market's columns. In this dataset 63% of markets resolved NO and 37% YES.

```{r}
markets <- read_parquet("data/markets.parquet")

joined <- open_dataset("data/history.parquet") |>
  collect() |>
  left_join(markets, by = "market_id") |>
  mutate(
    outcome_numeric  = if_else(outcome == "YES", 1, 0),
    prediction_error = abs(probability - outcome_numeric)
  )

groups        <- read_parquet("data/groups.parquet")
market_groups <- read_parquet("data/market_groups.parquet")

joined |>
  summarise(
    mean_error   = mean(prediction_error),
    median_error = median(prediction_error)
  )
```

###

`prediction_error` is measured in probability units from 0 to 1. The mean of 0.289 says the crowd sat about 29 percentage points from the truth across all snapshots — but that pools a forecast made six months out with one made on resolution day.

###

There are exactly 800 final-day rows, one per market, and 5,600 rows in the one-to-seven-day window, because each market can contribute up to seven of them. The timestamps arrive as text, as they usually do from a web API, and are in UTC, so a market resolving late in the evening in one country resolves the next day in the data.

### Exercise 6

The comparison to come is across time horizons, not individual days. In the same chunk, add a field that sorts each snapshot into one of five horizons — more than 90 days out, 30 to 90, 7 to 30, 1 to 7, and the final day — kept in chronological rather than alphabetical order. Count the rows in each to check the distribution. Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```r
show_file("analysis.qmd")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: crowd-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "The comparison to come is across time horizons, not individual days. In the same chunk, add a field that sorts each snapshot into one of five horizons — more than 90 days out, 30 to 90, 7 to 30, 1 to 7, and the final day — kept in chronological rather than alphabetical order. Count the rows in each to check the distribution. Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: crowd-6-answer
#| echo: true
markets <- read_parquet("data/markets.parquet")

joined <- open_dataset("data/history.parquet") |>
  collect() |>
  left_join(markets, by = "market_id") |>
  mutate(
    outcome_numeric    = if_else(outcome == "YES", 1, 0),
    prediction_error   = abs(probability - outcome_numeric),
    days_to_resolution = as.numeric(as.Date(ymd_hms(resolved_at)) - date),
    time_bucket = factor(
      case_when(
        days_to_resolution >  90 ~ "90+ days",
        days_to_resolution >  30 ~ "30–90 days",
        days_to_resolution >   7 ~ "7–30 days",
        days_to_resolution >=  1 ~ "1–7 days",
        TRUE                     ~ "Final day"
      ),
      levels = c("90+ days", "30–90 days", "7–30 days", "1–7 days", "Final day"),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

groups        <- read_parquet("data/groups.parquet")
market_groups <- read_parquet("data/market_groups.parquet")

joined |> count(time_bucket)
```

###

The 7–30 day bucket is the largest, with 16,467 rows, because the median market lives only 36 days and the longest 240. Storing the horizons as an ordered category rather than plain text is what keeps them in time order everywhere they are used; as text they would sort alphabetically and put "1–7 days" first.

The row count climbs from 800 to 2,885: the 2,820 group memberships contribute one row each, and the 65 markets with no group at all are kept by the left join as a single row apiece, so any per-market summary computed after this join would over-weight the markets carrying the most topic labels. That last point sits near zero but not on it, because a scatter of markets were still confidently wrong on their final day.

### Exercise 13

Convergence says markets get more accurate over time. The deeper question is whether they are well *calibrated* — whether events given a 70% chance actually happen about 70% of the time. Before testing that, look at the shape of the final-day forecasts. Leave the accuracy chart where it is and start a new chunk: filter `joined` to the snapshots on resolution day and plot the distribution of `probability`. Render.

Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: crowd-17
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Convergence says markets get more accurate over time. The deeper question is whether they are well calibrated — whether events given a 70% chance actually happen about 70% of the time. Before testing that, look at the shape of the final-day forecasts. Leave the accuracy chart where it is and start a new chunk: filter joined to the snapshots on resolution day and plot the distribution of probability. Render. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: crowd-17-answer
#| echo: true
joined |>
  filter(days_to_resolution == 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = probability)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#2166ac", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Final-day probability", y = "Number of markets",
       title = "Most markets resolve near certainty") +
  theme_minimal()
```

###

The distribution is sharply bimodal: of the 800 markets, 324 fall in the lowest bin and 182 in the highest by resolution day. That also tells you where the calibration test will be weak — the middle of the range has only a handful of markets each, because genuine uncertainty rarely survives to the final day.

### Exercise 14

Build the calibration table from those final-day snapshots. Group the markets into probability bins ten percentage points wide, and for each bin compute the fraction that actually resolved YES (`actual_rate`) along with the number of markets (`n`). Save the result as `calibration` and print it. Render.

In the R Terminal, run:


```{r}
#| label: crowd-19-answer
#| echo: true
calibration <- joined |>
  filter(days_to_resolution == 0) |>
  mutate(prob_bin = round(probability * 10) / 10) |>
  group_by(prob_bin) |>
  summarise(actual_rate = mean(outcome_numeric), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

calibration |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prob_bin, y = actual_rate)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  geom_line(color = "#2166ac") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), color = "#2166ac", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Predicted probability", y = "Actual resolution rate",
       title = "Calibration is tight at the extremes and noisy in between",
       subtitle = "Point size shows how many markets landed in each probability bin",
       size = "Markets") +
  theme_minimal()
```

###

The large dots at 0 and 1, where most of the data lives, sit almost exactly on the line — 0.5% of the bottom bin resolved YES and 99.5% of the top one. The middle is a different story: the middle bins hold between 11 and 67 markets, they zigzag across the diagonal, and the 70–90% bins all sit *above* it, at 92%, 91%, and 100%.

A final-day price is not magic; it is a market incorporating facts that often did not exist weeks earlier. These are also play-money markets on one platform over eight months, so the convergence result is about Manifold in this window, not about prediction markets in general.

## Summary

This tutorial covered key concepts from [Chapter 22: Arrow](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/arrow.html), [Chapter 19: Joins](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/joins.html), and [Chapter 17: Dates and times](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/datetimes.html) from [*R for Data Science (2e)*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund.

You read parquet files with **arrow**, inspected a schema before pulling anything into memory, joined market metadata onto a daily snapshot series, survived a many-to-many join through a junction table, and turned timestamps into an ordered factor of time horizons. The two charts you will publish answer different questions: mean error by horizon shows that forecasts *sharpen* toward the deadline, and the calibration curve shows where the stated probabilities can be *trusted*.

````{verbatim}
```{r}
#| cache: true
markets <- read_parquet("data/markets.parquet")

joined <- open_dataset("data/history.parquet") |>
  collect() |>
  left_join(markets, by = "market_id") |>
  mutate(
    outcome_numeric    = if_else(outcome == "YES", 1, 0),
    prediction_error   = abs(probability - outcome_numeric),
    days_to_resolution = as.numeric(as.Date(ymd_hms(resolved_at)) - date),
    time_bucket = factor(
      case_when(
        days_to_resolution >  90 ~ "90+ days",
        days_to_resolution >  30 ~ "30–90 days",
        days_to_resolution >   7 ~ "7–30 days",
        days_to_resolution >=  1 ~ "1–7 days",
        TRUE                     ~ "Final day"
      ),
      levels = c("90+ days", "30–90 days", "7–30 days", "1–7 days", "Final day"),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

groups        <- read_parquet("data/groups.parquet")
market_groups <- read_parquet("data/market_groups.parquet")
```

```{r}
accuracy <- joined |>
  group_by(time_bucket) |>
  summarise(mean_error = mean(prediction_error), n_rows = n(), .groups = "drop")

accuracy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time_bucket, y = mean_error, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "#2166ac") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#2166ac") +
  labs(
    title    = "Prediction markets get smarter near the deadline",
    subtitle = "Mean absolute error in Manifold Markets forecasts, by days remaining",
    x        = "Days until resolution",
    y        = "Mean absolute error"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
````

###

A forecaster who says 50% about everything is perfectly calibrated and useless; one who commits to 5% and 95% is far more informative but easier to embarrass. Manifold's curve is tight at the extremes, where most markets sit, and wanders in the middle, where few do — which is the shape you would expect when the interesting questions are also the rare ones.
